property_summary: Calling withdrawAll succeeds in transferring contract balance only when msg.sender equals C.owner()
withdrawAll can only succeed (not revert) when the caller equals C.owner()

Only the owner can make the contract transfer its entire balance to an arbitrary recipient (i.e., withdrawAll succeeds when and only when tx.origin/caller equals owner, not merely equal to recipient).
Only calls where msg.sender equals the contract's owner are allowed to successfully withdrawAll (calls from other senders must revert).
If a call to withdrawAll does not revert, then msg.sender equals the contract's owner.
If withdrawAll succeeds then the recipient passed equals the contract's owner (i.e., only the owner can be the beneficiary of a successful withdrawAll).

If withdrawAll succeeds (does not revert) then the recipient passed is equal to the caller OR the caller is the contract owner (in original only owner can succeed, so any successful call implies caller==owner), but the rule we assert: if it did not revert then msg.sender == c.owner().

For all inputs, only the contract owner can successfully withdraw the contract balance to a recipient; the mutant that requires msg.sender==_recipient (instead of owner) will allow a non-owner recipient caller to withdraw when caller==recipient, violating the ownership-only withdraw rule for some inputs.

For any caller and any recipient, only the owner (the address given at construction) can successfully cause withdrawAll to transfer the contract balance; the mutant that requires msg.sender==_recipient instead allows a non-owner recipient who calls for themselves to withdraw, so there exist inputs (caller == recipient != owner and contract has balance) that make the mutant succeed while the reference only allows owner calls.

For every caller and recipient, only the constructor-set owner can successfully withdraw the contract balance; the mutant that requires msg.sender==_recipient allows a non-owner recipient who calls for themselves to withdraw (caller==recipient!=owner) and thus violates this property for some inputs.

For every caller and recipient, if the caller is not the owner then withdrawAll(recipient) must revert (only the owner may withdraw); the mutant allowing caller==recipient lets a non-owner who is also the recipient withdraw, violating this rule for inputs where caller==recipient!=owner and the contract has balance.

For every caller and recipient, withdrawAll(recipient) can only succeed when msg.sender == owner (the constructor-set owner); the mutant that checks msg.sender == recipient instead allows a non-owner recipient who calls for themselves to withdraw, so there exist inputs (caller == recipient != owner with contract balance) where the mutant succeeds but the reference does not.
After owner calls withdrawAll transferring all contract balance, the recipient cannot reenter to drain additional funds so that address(c).balance == 0 holds.
Calling withdrawAll should not revert when msg.sender equals the contract's owner (so owner can always withdraw), i.e., if the caller is owner then withdrawAll must succeed.
If withdrawAll is called by the contract owner when C holds a positive balance, the call must not revert (i.e., owner can always successfully withdraw the contract's entire balance).
When withdrawAll is invoked by the contract owner, the call must not revert (i.e., owner can always successfully withdraw the contract's entire balance).
If the caller is the contract owner and C has a positive balance, withdrawAll must not revert (owner can successfully withdraw the entire balance).

For any recipient, when the owner calls withdrawAll the reference contract always sends all contract balance successfully (leaving c.balance == 0), whereas the mutant that uses low-level call may fail to transfer to a reverting/failing recipient causing c.balance != 0 for some recipient.

For any recipient contract that may revert on receive, the correct contract C using transfer will always leave its balance = 0 after the owner calls withdrawAll(recipient) (transfer forwards 2300 gas and will revert on recipient revert), while the mutant using low-level call that forwards 0 gas and checks ok can fail to transfer (leaving c.balance > 0) for some adversarial recipient — so assert address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll by owner.

For any recipient and any deposited balance, when the owner calls withdrawAll(recipient) the reference contract always drains its entire balance (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that uses a low-gas low-level call can fail to transfer to a recipient that requires gas, leaving address(c).balance > 0 for some adversarial recipient.

For every recipient contract that DOES NOT consume all gas in a payable fallback/receive (i.e., its fallback accepts the call without reverting but performs a gas-consuming loop), the reference using transfer (which forwards 2300 gas) still succeeds in transferring the full balance (so c.balance == 0 after owner withdrawAll), but the mutant that forwards 0 gas can fail to send to such a recipient (leaving address(c).balance > 0); the test fuzzes a transferedBalance and uses an adversarial recipient that accepts but requires >0 gas to credit funds, causing the mutant to fail while the reference still empties c.

For every recipient that MAY revert when receiving Ether, the reference contract's transfer will revert the whole withdrawAll call only if the recipient reverts, ensuring that after a successful withdrawAll by the owner the contract balance is zero; the mutant that uses a low-level call forwarding 0 gas can report failure (ok == false) and leave funds in the contract for some adversarial recipient, thus violating the property that owner-withdraw always results in address(c).balance == 0 for all non-reverting recipient behaviors.
After owner calls withdrawAll(recipient) the recipient's balance increases by exactly the contract balance that existed just before the call.
withdrawAll called by any non-owner always reverts (i.e., only the owner can successfully call withdrawAll).
If caller is not the owner of c then calling c.withdrawAll(recipient) must revert (i.e., (caller != c.owner()) == reverted).
If caller is not the owner of c then calling c.withdrawAll(recipient) must revert (i.e., (caller != c.owner()) == reverted).
If caller is not the owner of c then calling c.withdrawAll(recipient) must revert (i.e., (caller != c.owner()) == reverted).

For any recipient address and any starting contract balance funded by the caller, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the recipient (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that first transfers 0 then transfers the balance can cause the final contract balance to be non-zero when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts, breaking this rule.

For any recipient and any starting ether funding sent into C via withdrawAll, the reference contract always ends with address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll returns; the mutant that first sends 0 then transfers the balance can let the recipient's fallback revert during the second transfer causing the call to behave differently and leave address(c).balance != 0 for some recipient behaviors.

For any recipient contract that may revert when receiving ether and any initial funding amount, the correct contract C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll(recipient) returns, whereas the mutant that first transfers 0 then transfers the balance can leave address(c).balance != 0 when the recipient reverts on the second transfer.

For any recipient contract and any starting ether funded into C by the caller via withdrawAll, the reference C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll returns; the mutant that does a harmless zero-value transfer before transferring the balance can cause the second transfer to revert on a malicious recipient and leave address(c).balance > 0 for some inputs (recipient behavior), so the property is that address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll completes.

For any recipient contract that can accept a zero-value transfer successfully but that REVERTS when receiving a nonzero value, the reference C always leaves address(c).balance == 0 after withdrawAll(recipient) (because the single transfer of the full balance either succeeds or reverts the whole call), whereas the mutant that issues a zero-value transfer first can make the subsequent nonzero transfer revert while the earlier zero-value transfer already executed, leaving address(c).balance > 0 for some recipient behaviors.
Only the recorded owner can cause the contract C to transfer its entire balance out (i.e., withdrawAll succeeds in moving funds only when called by owner).

If the caller is not the recorded owner, withdrawAll must revert (non-owners cannot successfully withdraw contract balance).
If the supplied caller address is different from the on-chain owner getter, then the call to withdrawAll must revert.
If the provided caller address is different from the on-chain owner, then calling withdrawAll must revert (non-owners cannot successfully invoke withdrawAll).

Invariant: Only the owner address may successfully transfer out the contract balance via withdrawAll(address) — the reference enforces this for every caller; the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to drain the contract, so for some caller addresses the mutant will succeed while the reference will not.
